records.sourceFile: Inter-limb asymmetry in youth elite soccer players - Effect of loading conditions.pdf

paper.citation: Ascenzi G, Filetti C, Di Salvo V, et al. Inter-limb asymmetry in youth elite soccer players: Effect of loading conditions. PLOS ONE. 2022;17(6):e0269695.
paper.abstract: This experimental study examined whether inter-limb strength asymmetry changes with test and load conditions. Fifteen elite youth soccer players performed rear-foot-elevated split squats under three external loads plus isokinetic knee-flexor and knee-extensor assessments.
paper.tldr: The size and favored side of inter-limb asymmetry changed across loads and test modes in 15 elite youth players. An asymmetry score is specific to how it was measured; one percentage should not become a stable athlete label or universal injury threshold.
paper.methods: Players completed split-squat tests with body mass, an additional 25% of body mass, and an additional 50% of body mass, along with concentric and eccentric isokinetic tests. Agreement statistics compared the magnitude and direction of asymmetry between conditions.
paper.findings: Agreement was moderate only between the body-mass and body-mass-plus-25% split-squat conditions and was fair or absent for most other comparisons. Both asymmetry magnitude and the limb identified as lower performing were inconsistent across loads and assessments.
paper.limitations: The sample was small, male, and drawn from one academy; testing was cross-sectional and no injury or future-performance outcomes were tracked. The findings do not validate a diagnostic threshold or show that reducing asymmetry improves outcomes.
paper.practicalImplications: Standardize the task, load, range, and metric when monitoring asymmetry and interpret change within that exact test. Confirm an unusual result across repeated sessions and relevant tasks before changing a program.
paper.athleteDev: Select unilateral tests that match the physical quality and loading context of interest. Use asymmetry as descriptive information alongside bilateral capacity and sport performance, not as the sole target of training.
paper.rtp: During rehabilitation, reproduce the same test conditions when tracking side-to-side recovery. Clearance should not depend on one asymmetry percentage or on a side designation that may change with task and load.

records.sourceFile: Is hip adductor or abductor strength in healthy athletes associated with future groin pain - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Quintana-Cepedal M, Vicente-Rodríguez G, Crespo I, Olmedillas H. Is hip adductor or abductor strength in healthy athletes associated with future groin pain? A systematic review and meta-analysis. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2025;59(7):501-509.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined prospective associations between preseason hip adductor or abductor strength and later groin pain or time-loss injury in healthy athletes. Thirteen cohort studies were included and evidence certainty was assessed with GRADE.
paper.tldr: Lower hip-adductor strength had a moderate, low-certainty association with future groin pain across 13 cohorts. Abductor strength and the adductor-to-abductor ratio were not associated, and the review does not establish a predictive cut point.
paper.methods: Six databases were searched for prospective studies that measured hip strength before follow-up and separately reported athletes who remained healthy or developed groin pain. Risk of bias used QUIPS and pooled standardized effects were evaluated with evidence-certainty grading.
paper.findings: Athletes who remained uninjured had greater baseline adductor strength than those who later developed groin pain. Pooled findings did not support associations for abductor strength or the adductor-to-abductor ratio, and diagnostic criteria were not a significant moderator.
paper.limitations: Strength tests, diagnostic criteria, follow-up periods, sports, and reporting varied, the adductor finding was low certainty, and female athletes made up only about 3% of the sample. Association does not establish prevention or an individual risk probability.
paper.practicalImplications: Adductor strength is reasonable to include in a broader groin-health assessment, particularly as a repeatable within-athlete measure. Avoid categorical high-risk labels or decisions based on the strength ratio alone.
paper.athleteDev: Develop adequate adductor capacity as part of comprehensive lower-body preparation, but do not chase a universal ratio. Interpret strength alongside prior symptoms, exposure, training history, and movement demands.
paper.rtp: Adductor strength can document recovery from groin problems, but this review does not provide a clearance threshold. Combine it with pain, clinical examination, change-of-direction and kicking exposure, and full training tolerance.

records.sourceFile: The effect of fixture congestion on performance during professional male soccer match play - A systematic critical review with meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Julian R, Page RM, Harper LD. The effect of fixture congestion on performance during professional male soccer match-play: A systematic critical review with meta-analysis. Sports Medicine. 2021;51(2):255-273.
paper.abstract: This systematic critical review evaluated physical, technical, and tactical performance during congested professional male soccer schedules, defined as successive matches separated by less than 96 hours. Sixteen studies were reviewed and five contributed total-distance data to meta-analysis.
paper.tldr: Fixture congestion did not meaningfully reduce total match distance in the pooled analysis, but other physical outcomes were inconsistent and tactical evidence was sparse. Stable distance does not prove complete recovery or unchanged individual performance.
paper.methods: Three databases were searched under a preregistered PRISMA process. Eligible studies involved professional male players, at least two matches within 96 hours, and physical, technical, or tactical match outcomes; total distance was the only consistently pooled variable.
paper.findings: The pooled standardized effect for total distance was not significant and heterogeneity was moderate. Physical findings outside total distance were equivocal, technical performance was generally maintained, and one available tactical study suggested possible impairment.
paper.limitations: Few outcomes were measured consistently, several studies had weak designs, and player rotation, opposition, match importance, travel, position, and substitution could confound results. The review included only professional men.
paper.practicalImplications: Plan congested periods with individual exposure, high-intensity actions, travel, wellness, and tactical demands in view rather than relying on total distance alone. Rotation and recovery support remain contextual decisions.
paper.athleteDev: Prepare players for repeated-match demands while preserving training quality between fixtures. Use position- and athlete-specific response to determine whether maintenance, recovery, or top-up work is appropriate.
paper.rtp: A returning athlete may have lower congestion tolerance than a fully available player even when match distance appears normal. Progress repeated exposures deliberately and use symptoms, function, and recovery response rather than schedule alone.

records.sourceFile: The Effect of Training Loads on Performance Measures and Injury Characteristics in Rugby League Players- A Systematic Review.pdf

paper.citation: Booth M, Orr R, Cobley S. The effect of training loads on performance measures and injury characteristics in rugby league players: A systematic review. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2018;13(10):1259-1272.
paper.abstract: This systematic review examined training-load relationships with physical performance and injury characteristics in rugby league. Five databases were searched through December 2016 and 12 studies with quantified load and performance or injury outcomes were included.
paper.tldr: Higher rugby-league training loads were associated with both selected fitness improvements and more injury in a heterogeneous 12-study literature. The evidence does not identify one optimal or harmful workload threshold.
paper.methods: The PRISMA-guided search included studies using measures such as session rating of perceived exertion with physical-performance tests or injury surveillance. Results were synthesized across preseason and in-season contexts.
paper.findings: The highest loads generally occurred in preseason. Higher loads accompanied improvements in aerobic power, jump, and agility outcomes but were also associated with strains, sprains, lower-limb injuries, and overuse or overexertion problems.
paper.limitations: Definitions, load metrics, age and competitive levels, performance tests, injury surveillance, and study designs varied. The primarily observational evidence cannot isolate causality or establish a universal dose-response curve.
paper.practicalImplications: Evaluate load as both an adaptation stimulus and an exposure cost. Make decisions from absolute work, progression, recent history, athlete response, and available recovery rather than a single ratio or threshold.
paper.athleteDev: Progress collision, running, and conditioning demands with the target adaptation explicit. Fitness development and injury exposure can rise together, so greater workload is neither automatically good nor automatically unsafe.
paper.rtp: Reconditioning should rebuild rugby-specific load progressively without using population associations as clearance rules. Track symptoms, contact tolerance, physical capacity, and repeated training exposure.

records.sourceFile: Detrimental effects of the off-season in soccer players - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Clemente FM, Ramirez-Campillo R, Sarmento H. Detrimental effects of the off-season in soccer players: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Sports Medicine. 2021;51(4):795-814.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated at least two weeks of training cessation or off-season training in healthy male soccer players. Twelve studies reported body composition, aerobic fitness, intermittent-running, jumping, sprinting, or repeated-sprint outcomes.
paper.tldr: Complete off-season cessation produced meaningful losses across several fitness qualities, while off-season programs attenuated declines in VO2max and repeated-sprint ability. Even trained groups lost some qualities, so maintenance programs reduce rather than eliminate detraining.
paper.methods: Controlled trials and cohorts with pre-post off-season measures were pooled by outcome. Comparisons examined training cessation and off-season programs for body fat, VO2max, Yo-Yo performance, jumping, sprint time, and repeated-sprint ability.
paper.findings: Training cessation worsened body fat, VO2max, Yo-Yo performance, vertical jump, and repeated-sprint ability. Off-season programs also showed some losses but produced smaller declines than cessation for VO2max and repeated-sprint ability.
paper.limitations: Studies involved males, used varied program content and durations, and included different ages and competition levels with small samples and inconsistent control. The review cannot prescribe one ideal off-season dose.
paper.practicalImplications: Use a low-burden off-season plan that maintains key aerobic, sprint, and strength exposures while allowing psychological and physical recovery. Select the minimum effective work for the athlete's next reporting date and needs.
paper.athleteDev: Avoid both extremes of uninterrupted high load and complete inactivity. Maintain important qualities with flexible, individualized exposures and plan a progressive return into preseason.
paper.rtp: Athletes returning from injury need individualized off-season work rather than the healthy-player template. Preserve rehabilitation continuity and account for detraining before resuming team preseason loads.

records.sourceFile: Adductor strengthening program is successfully adopted but frequently modified in Norwegian male professional soccer teams - A cross-sectional study.pdf

paper.citation: Stensø J, Andersen TE, Harøy J. Adductor Strengthening Programme is successfully adopted but frequently modified in Norwegian male professional football teams: A cross-sectional study. BMJ Open. 2022;12(9):e060611.
paper.abstract: This cross-sectional RE-AIM survey examined adoption and real-world use of the Adductor Strengthening Programme among delivery agents in the top two Norwegian male professional football divisions. Twenty-nine of 32 invited practitioners responded.
paper.tldr: Practitioners widely knew and adopted the Adductor Strengthening Programme, but only 10% delivered the original protocol. Implementation success should include fidelity and active dose, not just whether a team says it uses the program.
paper.methods: A questionnaire mapped awareness, adoption, implementation, effectiveness beliefs, and maintenance intentions across the five RE-AIM dimensions. Respondents also described common protocol changes and one professional-team application was documented.
paper.findings: All respondents were aware of and had adopted the program, 97% intended to continue, and the injury-prevention evidence and lack of equipment were valued. Only 10% used the original protocol, with common changes to frequency, progression, and delivery.
paper.limitations: The survey was self-reported, cross-sectional, and limited to one country's male professional system. Fidelity was not directly observed and player exposure or injury outcomes were not linked to the modified versions.
paper.practicalImplications: When implementing an evidence-based program, record what was actually completed and why it changed. Audit frequency, progression, intensity, reach, and maintenance rather than counting program adoption alone.
paper.athleteDev: Adaptations may be necessary in a team setting, but preserve the mechanism and sufficient dose. Review modifications with performance and medical staff so convenience does not silently remove the active ingredients.
paper.rtp: This study addressed primary prevention implementation, not return-to-sport treatment. A modified program should not be assumed to reproduce either the trial's prevention effect or an individualized rehabilitation plan.

records.sourceFile: Proximal, Distal, and Contralateral Effects of Blood Flow Restriction Training on the Lower Extremities- A Randomized Controlled Tria.pdf

paper.citation: Bowman EN, Elshaar R, Milligan H, et al. Proximal, distal, and contralateral effects of blood flow restriction training on the lower extremities: A randomized controlled trial. Sports Health. 2019;11(2):149-156.
paper.abstract: This randomized controlled trial evaluated six weeks of unilateral low-load blood-flow-restriction training in healthy adults. Sixteen BFR and 10 control participants completed strength testing and limb-circumference measurements before and after training.
paper.tldr: Low-load BFR increased strength and limb circumference around the trained limb, with smaller gains in the noncuffed limb and no reported adverse events in 26 screened healthy adults. The small healthy sample does not establish safety or effectiveness in injured athletes.
paper.methods: Participants were randomized to unilateral BFR training or control and completed a standardized six-week protocol. Isokinetic torque, work, power, and thigh and leg circumference were compared within and between the cuffed, contralateral, and control limbs.
paper.findings: The BFR group improved knee-extension torque, work, power, and limb circumference more than controls. Proximal, distal, and smaller contralateral improvements were observed, and no adverse events were reported during the study.
paper.limitations: Only 26 healthy young adults completed the trial, medical-risk groups and previously operated limbs were excluded, and follow-up was short. Circumference is an imprecise hypertrophy measure and adverse-event absence in this sample is not broad safety proof.
paper.practicalImplications: BFR can provide a low-load strengthening option when high loads are not desirable, but requires appropriate screening, individualized cuff pressure, supervision, and documentation of symptoms and response.
paper.athleteDev: Use BFR as an adjunct for a specific loading constraint, not a default replacement for progressive high-load training. Transition toward task-relevant loading as tolerance and goals allow.
paper.rtp: BFR may support capacity during rehabilitation, but this healthy-adult study does not supply postoperative protocols or clearance criteria. Clinical risk screening and tissue-specific progression remain essential.

records.sourceFile: The Adductor Strengthening Programme prevents groin problems among male football players- a cluster-randomised controlled tria.pdf

paper.citation: Harøy J, Clarsen B, Wiger EG, et al. The Adductor Strengthening Programme prevents groin problems among male football players: A cluster-randomised controlled trial. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2019;53(3):150-157.
paper.abstract: This cluster-randomized trial tested a single-exercise progressive Copenhagen-adduction program in 35 Norwegian semiprofessional male football teams. The intervention included three weekly preseason sessions for six to eight weeks and one weekly in-season session for 28 weeks.
paper.tldr: The studied adductor program reduced average weekly groin-problem prevalence from 21.3% to 13.5%, a 41% relative reduction. The effect belongs to this progressive protocol and male semiprofessional setting, not every modified Copenhagen routine.
paper.methods: Eighteen teams with 339 players were assigned to the program and 17 teams with 313 players continued normal training. Weekly groin problems were measured during the competitive season with the Oslo Sports Trauma Research Center Overuse Injury Questionnaire.
paper.findings: Average weekly groin-problem prevalence was 13.5% in the intervention group and 21.3% in controls. The relative risk of reporting any groin problem was 41% lower, while the reduction in substantial groin problems was smaller and not statistically significant.
paper.limitations: Teams and athletes could not be blinded, adherence varied, outcomes were self-reported, and the setting was male semiprofessional football. The trial does not establish equal effects in women, youth, other sports, or altered protocols.
paper.practicalImplications: Use the simple progressive program as a team-level groin-prevention option and protect the studied frequency and progression. Monitor adherence, soreness, and actual weekly exposure.
paper.athleteDev: Build adductor strength before and throughout the competitive season with progressive Copenhagen-adduction exposure. Integrate it with the rest of the lower-body program so dosage is sustainable.
paper.rtp: The protocol was preventive, not a treatment or clearance pathway for current groin pain. Symptomatic athletes require individualized assessment and graded rehabilitation before joining the team dose.

records.sourceFile: The effect of cannabidiol on subjective responses to endurance exercise - A randomized controlled trial.pdf

paper.citation: McCartney D, Irwin C, Bawa Z, et al. The effect of cannabidiol on subjective responses to endurance exercise: A randomised controlled trial. Sports Medicine - Open. 2024;10(1):61.
paper.abstract: This randomized double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial examined whether 150 mg oral cannabidiol changed subjective experience or performance during a self-paced 10 km track run. Fifty-one recreationally active adults completed the analysis.
paper.tldr: A single 150 mg CBD dose did not improve affect, enjoyment, motivation, runner's-high features, perceived exertion, pain, or 10 km time. The trial provides no acute endurance-experience benefit and does not address other doses, chronic use, recovery, or treatment.
paper.methods: Participants took CBD or placebo 90 minutes before each 10 km trial in randomized crossover order. Repeated measures assessed affective valence, positive and negative affect, enjoyment, motivation, self-efficacy, euphoria, pain, anxiety, sedation, perceived effort, and run time.
paper.findings: Exercise produced expected changes in affect and pain, but CBD did not significantly affect any measured subjective outcome or running performance compared with placebo.
paper.limitations: The sample was young and recreational, the study tested one acute dose and product, and several outcomes were self-reported. Results do not establish long-term safety, recovery effects, clinical benefit, or responses in elite athletes.
paper.practicalImplications: Do not recommend CBD to improve the immediate subjective endurance experience or performance based on this trial. Product quality, health, medication interactions, policy, and anti-doping risk remain separate considerations.
paper.athleteDev: CBD should not displace established endurance preparation, pacing, fueling, recovery, or psychological strategies. A null result is not evidence of broader safety or effectiveness.
paper.rtp: The trial studied healthy recreational exercise and offers no return-to-sport evidence. CBD use should not influence clearance or symptom-readiness decisions.

records.sourceFile: Acute effects of training loads on muscle damage markers and performance in semi-elite and elite athletes - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Simmons R, Doma K, Sinclair W, Connor J, Leicht A. Acute effects of training loads on muscle damage markers and performance in semi-elite and elite athletes: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Sports Medicine. 2021;51(10):2181-2207.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated acute muscle-damage markers and performance responses to periodized training in semi-elite and elite athletes. Thirty-two studies compared preseason with off-season, similar seasonal loads, or acute increases and decreases in load.
paper.tldr: Creatine kinase generally rose early in preseason and moved with acute training-load changes, while other inflammatory and performance responses were inconsistent. CK is a context-sensitive group signal, not an individual readiness diagnosis.
paper.methods: Five databases were searched for studies of acute response to training in periodized semi-elite or elite programs. Kmet quality appraisal was used and compatible data were pooled for creatine kinase and related outcomes with heterogeneity assessment.
paper.findings: CK and indirect damage signals were higher in early preseason than off-season, did not differ consistently at two comparable-load time points, and rose or fell alongside acute load changes. Other inflammatory and performance results were inconclusive.
paper.limitations: Age, sex, sport, competition level, training load, biomarker timing, and outcomes varied, and several pooled analyses had substantial heterogeneity. Group averages cannot define individual damage, recovery, or a safe load threshold.
paper.practicalImplications: If CK is used, standardize collection and interpret within-athlete change alongside recent load, soreness, performance, illness, and baseline variability. Do not make readiness decisions from CK alone.
paper.athleteDev: Expect a larger response when load is reintroduced or increased and progress preseason work accordingly. Use performance and athlete response to decide whether adaptation is occurring as intended.
paper.rtp: A biomarker response during reconditioning may add context but cannot determine tissue healing or clearance. Progression still depends on symptoms, function, sport exposure, and clinical judgment.

records.sourceFile: Career outlook and performance of professional athletes after Achilles tendon rupture - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Johns W, Walley KC, Seedat R, Thordarson DB, Jackson B, Gonzalez T. Career outlook and performance of professional athletes after Achilles tendon rupture: A systematic review. Foot & Ankle International. 2021;42(4):495-509.
paper.abstract: This systematic review examined return, performance, participation, and career outcomes after Achilles tendon rupture in professional NFL, NBA, MLB, and soccer athletes. Fifteen studies met the inclusion criteria.
paper.tldr: About 76% of professional athletes returned after Achilles rupture at an average of 11 months, and returning players often had reduced performance or durability. These league-level averages set expectations but are not individual timelines or clearance criteria.
paper.methods: MEDLINE, Google Scholar, CINAHL, and Cochrane Library were searched for professional-sport studies reporting time and rate of return, durability, participation, or postrupture performance.
paper.findings: Professional athletes returned 76% of the time after a mean 11 months. Efficiency, power, and sport- or position-specific metrics often declined compared with preinjury values or noninjured controls, and return rates were lower than for several other orthopedic injuries.
paper.limitations: The evidence was retrospective and heterogeneous across leagues, eras, treatments, rehabilitation, and performance metrics. Public-data selection, survivor bias, and limited female professional evidence restrict individualized prognosis.
paper.practicalImplications: Discuss both probability and quality of return: clearance may precede full restoration of workload, performance, and career durability. Plan progression and support beyond the initial return date.
paper.athleteDev: Rebuild plantar-flexor capacity, elastic qualities, high-speed exposure, and sport-specific actions over a long horizon. Expect performance restoration to continue after return to participation.
paper.rtp: The 76% return rate and 11-month mean are expectation-setting benchmarks only. Individual decisions require healing, calf and tendon function, strength and power, running and change-of-direction exposure, confidence, and full training tolerance.

records.sourceFile: Effects of training and competition on the sleep of elite athletes- a systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Roberts SSH, Teo WP, Warmington SA. Effects of training and competition on the sleep of elite athletes: A systematic review and meta-analysis. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2019;53(8):513-522.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis characterized objectively measured sleep in elite athletes and training or competition factors associated with poorer sleep. Fifty-four observational studies reported total sleep time or sleep efficiency.
paper.tldr: Elite athletes frequently obtained less sleep than common recommendations, especially around competition. Early training, abrupt load increases, late or early travel, eastward travel, and altitude were recurring schedule-level risks that staff can modify.
paper.methods: PubMed, Scopus, and SPORTDiscus were searched through February 2018 for observational elite-athlete studies with objective total-sleep-time or sleep-efficiency data. Competition nights and identified training or travel factors were compared with preceding conditions.
paper.findings: Many studies reported inadequate sleep time or efficiency during training and competition. Competition nights averaged about 60 fewer minutes of sleep, night competitions about 80 fewer minutes, and early training, load increases above 25%, difficult travel timing, eastward travel, and altitude were associated with impairment.
paper.limitations: Studies were predominantly observational and heterogeneous in sport, device, schedule, and sleep criteria, with limited control of individual chronotype and environment. Group recommendation thresholds do not define each athlete's sleep requirement.
paper.practicalImplications: Protect sleep opportunity through schedule design: reconsider very early sessions, build load progressively, and plan postcompetition and travel timing. Combine objective trends with athlete report and daytime function.
paper.athleteDev: Teach athletes to anticipate high-risk nights and use consistent routines, light timing, naps, and recovery planning where appropriate. Focus on sustainable opportunity and response rather than one universal target.
paper.rtp: Sleep supports recovery but is not a standalone clearance criterion. During rehabilitation, address schedule barriers and interpret sleep alongside symptoms, function, mood, and training tolerance.
